title: The potter (Jeremiah 18)
hookLine: a vessel spoiled in the potter's hand is made again

lines: ONE WOBBLE, AND THE BOWL FOLDS.
GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.
A PROPHET WATCHES A POT FAIL.
cards: Anyone who has tried a pottery class knows the moment. The clay is spinning, it's rising, it actually looks like a bowl, and then one wobble and the whole wall folds over like a tired flower.
The instructor doesn't hand you new clay. She says: squash it, wet it, center it again. Jeremiah watched that moment about twenty-six centuries ago.
God sent him on an errand with no explanation: go down to the potter's house, and you'll hear my words there. So he stood in a workshop and watched a craftsman ruin a pot.

teach.h: THE VESSEL SPOILED ON THE WHEEL.
teach.b: The potter is at his wheel, and the vessel he's shaping goes wrong in his hands. He doesn't throw the clay out.

teach.h: HE MAKES ANOTHER FROM THE SAME CLAY.
teach.b: He gathers it up and makes another vessel from the same lump, as it seemed good to him. Then the word comes, a question first: can't I do with you what this potter does?
And in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel." Two things are true at once in that workshop. The clay is soft, so it can go wrong.
And because it's still soft, it can be made again. A word is hiding here from yesterday.

The Hebrew for potter, yotser, means one who forms, from the same verb as before I formed thee. The God who formed Jeremiah in the womb is the potter still at the wheel. The message wasn't only comfort, though.
The next verses warn a whole nation: if a people turns from its evil, God will relent; if it turns from good, the good is taken back.
And in the next chapter Jeremiah buys a finished, fired jar and smashes it in front of the elders.

teach.h: A FIRED JAR CAN'T BE REWORKED.
teach.b: A fired pot can't be reworked. Many Catholics think of this chapter when they bring what has gone wrong to God, in the sacrament of penance, in an evening examen, in a quiet church.

teach.h: AS CLAY IS IN THE HAND OF THE POTTER.
teach.b: The pot that slumped isn't the end of the clay.

how: Catholics bring what has gone wrong in their lives to God in the sacrament of penance and in daily prayer, and Jeremiah's visit to the potter's house is among the readings at weekday Mass.

games.why: he makes another vessel from the same clay, as it seemed good to him. then God asks: can't I do with you as this potter does?

practice: Cup your hands in your lap as if you were holding a lump of wet clay, and let something that went wrong come to mind: a conversation that collapsed, a habit that slumped, a plan that folded on the wheel.
Don't fix it; just hold it, and notice it's still soft. If you pray, hold your hands out and give it back to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: The potter. In Jeremiah, the craftsman who doesn't throw away spoiled clay but makes it into another vessel. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: potter, literally one who forms, from the same verb as before I formed thee (Jeremiah 1:5).

carryVoice: Your line: made again. Same clay, another vessel, still soft. That's day four hundred twenty-two.
